newsitem.title: USA: KDP does not rule out talks with Kurdish rivals.
newsitem.headline: KDP does not rule out talks with Kurdish rivals.

text.p: Officials of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) said on Thursday they did not exclude direct peace talks with their Kurdish rivals in northern Iraq, but wanted guarantees any agreement would be respected.

The officials were speaking before talks at the State Department, which this week launched a new initiative to end fighting between the KDP and the rival Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) in Western-protected northern Iraq.

Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs, Robert Pelletreau, will set out for the Middle East at the weekend for separate talks with the leaders of both groups, the State Department announced on Wednesday.

"We have never refused talks," said Sami Abdurrahman, head of the KDP delegation in Washington. But, he added, "talks must be protected also from violation. If somebody pledges to make talks and to make a cease-fire, then when he breaks the cease-fire he should be condemned, he should pay for it."
"I didn't say we are not willing (to talk to the PUK), but we want a guarantee that talks are talks," Abdurrahman told reporters.

Fighting which erupted between the two groups in August has seriously weakened the U.S. position in northern Iraq, forcing the evacuation of U.S. aid, military and intelligence operations and threatening to draw in Iraq and Iran.

The KDP invited in regular Iraqi forces to help it capture the key city of Arbil at the end of August. The KDP took control of most of the region, but a recent PUK counter-offensive has recaptured much of the territory.
Abdurrahman said his delegation expected to meet Pelletreau and Robert Deutsch, head of the State Department's Iran and Iraq desk.

He said they would discuss the protection of the Kurdish people, and the return of the allied Military Coordination Center, which handled liaison with the Kurds since the 1991 Gulf War, and the U.S. Office of Foreign Disaster Assistance.
Abdurrahman charged that it was the PUK which had started the latest round of fighting by breaking a cease-fire on Aug. 17.

He defended the KDP decision to invite help from Baghdad, saying it was to "counterbalance the Iranian aggression" in support of the PUK. Both Iran and the PUK have denied that Tehran is aiding the group.
KDP leader Massoud Barzani warned on Thursday in northern Iraq that he might again ask Baghdad for help against the PUK. Abdurrahman said he was unaware of Barzani's statement.
